evidence.excerpt: A central composite design was used to map the effect of barrel temperature (120–160 °C), screw speed (80–200 rpm), and sunflower protein concentrate content (0–25 wt%) on the mechanical and barrier properties of blown films produced from the extruded blends via a subsequent film blowing step. Seventeen experimental runs yielded response surfaces for tensile strength, elongation at break, Young's modulus, water vapour transmission rate (WVTR), and oxygen transmission rate (OTR). Tensile strength ranged from 7.2 to 16.8 MPa across the design space; OTR varied from 180 to 620 cm³·m⁻²·day⁻¹·bar⁻¹. Optimal conditions identified by desirability function (maximum strength and minimum OTR) were 148 °C, 145 rpm, and 18 wt% protein. At the optimum, predicted and experimental values agreed within 6%. Specific mechanical energy was modelled as a secondary response and found to increase linearly with screw speed but to show a quadratic relationship with protein content, with a minimum near 12 wt% attributed to lubrication effects of denatured protein at low concentration.
